cards.title: The price seesaw
cards.body: Supply is how much sellers want to sell; demand is how much buyers want to buy. When demand rises and supply stays put, prices climb. When supply floods in and demand stays flat, prices fall. Almost every price you see is this seesaw finding its balance.

cards.title: Equilibrium: where they meet
cards.body: The equilibrium price is where the amount sellers want to sell exactly matches what buyers want to buy. Below it, shortages — shelves empty. Above it, surpluses — goods pile up. Markets are constantly nudging toward this point, even if they rarely sit still on it.

A heatwave hits and everyone wants ice cream (demand jumps). Shops sell out at the old price, so they raise it. Higher prices tempt more suppliers to stock ice cream, and some buyers drop out — until supply and demand meet again, at a higher price than before.

When you see a price change, ask: did supply move, or did demand move? New iPhone launch with the same factories — demand moved. A drought hits coffee farms — supply moved. One question, and most price mysteries solve themselves.

cards.q: A drought destroys half the coffee crop. What happens to coffee prices?
choices: They rise — less supply at the same demand
cards.explain: Supply fell while demand stayed the same, so buyers compete for less coffee and bid the price up. Classic supply shift.

flashcards.front: What is supply? What is demand?
flashcards.back: Supply: how much sellers want to sell. Demand: how much buyers want to buy.
The price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.

flashcards.front: What happens below the equilibrium price?
flashcards.back: A shortage — buyers want more than sellers offer, so shelves empty.

flashcards.front: Demand for ice cream spikes in a heatwave. What happens to price?
flashcards.back: It rises until higher supply and lower demand meet the new balance.

questions.q: If supply increases while demand stays the same, prices tend to:
questions.explain: More supply chasing the same demand means sellers compete by cutting prices — a surplus pushes prices down.
Shortage = buyers want more than sellers provide at that price. It usually means the price is below equilibrium.

questions.q: Concert tickets sell out in minutes and resell for triple. The original price was:
questions.explain: Instant sellouts plus a thriving resale market scream shortage — the face price was set below what the market would bear.

questions.q: A new factory doubles the supply of sneakers. In the short run:
questions.explain: Supply shifted right with demand unchanged — the new equilibrium sits at a lower price and higher quantity.

questions.q: Why do economists say 'there's no such thing as a free lunch'?
choices: Every choice has an opportunity cost
questions.explain: Resources are scarce, so getting something means giving up the next-best alternative. That forgone value is the opportunity cost.

cards.title: Inflation: money gets thinner
cards.body: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time — your dollar buys a little less each year. A 3% inflation rate means something costing $100 today costs about $103 next year. A little inflation is normal; a lot of it quietly taxes everyone's savings.

cards.title: Interest: the price of money
cards.body: Interest is what you pay to borrow money — or what you're paid to lend it. When central banks raise interest rates, borrowing gets expensive: mortgages, car loans, and credit cards all cost more, which cools spending and slows inflation. Lower rates do the opposite.

You stash $1,000 under your mattress for 10 years at 3% annual inflation. When you dig it up, it buys what about $744 bought back then — you lost a quarter of your purchasing power doing nothing. Money sitting still is money shrinking.

Always compare interest rates to inflation. A savings account paying 1% while inflation runs 3% means your money is shrinking 2% a year in real terms. The real return is what matters: nominal rate minus inflation.

cards.q: Inflation is 4% and your savings pay 2%. What happens to your purchasing power?
cards.explain: Real return = nominal minus inflation: 2% − 4% = −2%. Your balance grows in dollars but buys less each year.

flashcards.back: A general rise in prices over time, so each dollar buys less.

flashcards.front: What does raising interest rates do?
flashcards.back: Makes borrowing expensive, cools spending, and slows inflation.

flashcards.front: How do you find the real return on savings?
flashcards.back: Nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate.

flashcards.front: $1,000 sits for 10 years at 3% inflation. What happens?
flashcards.back: It loses about a quarter of its purchasing power — buys what ~$744 bought before.

questions.q: If inflation is 5%, a $100 grocery basket next year costs about:
questions.explain: 5% of $100 is $5, so the same basket costs roughly $105. That's inflation eating your dollar.

questions.q: Why do central banks raise rates to fight inflation?
choices: Expensive borrowing slows spending, cooling price rises
questions.explain: Higher rates make loans and credit costly, so people and businesses spend less. Less spending pressure = slower price growth.

questions.q: Your bond pays 6% and inflation is 2%. Your real return is:
questions.explain: Real return ≈ nominal − inflation = 6% − 2% = 4%. That's the actual gain in purchasing power.

questions.q: Deflation (falling prices) sounds nice. Why do economists fear it?
choices: People delay buying, which can stall the whole economy
questions.explain: If prices will be lower tomorrow, everyone waits — spending collapses, businesses cut jobs, and the spiral feeds itself.

questions.q: Who is hurt most by unexpected high inflation?
choices: Lenders and people holding cash savings
questions.explain: Inflation shrinks what money is worth, so cash-holders and fixed-rate lenders lose. Borrowers actually benefit — they repay with cheaper dollars.

cards.title: Stocks are slices of companies
cards.body: A stock is a tiny ownership slice of a company. Buy a share and you own a fraction of its future profits — which is why prices rise when the company does well and fall when it stumbles. You're not betting on a number; you're buying a piece of a business.

cards.title: Risk and return hold hands
cards.body: In markets, higher potential returns always come with higher risk — there are no exceptions, only sales pitches. A savings account is safe and pays little; a startup stock might 10x or go to zero. Anyone promising high returns with no risk is selling you something.

You buy 10 shares at $50 each ($500 total). The company thrives and shares hit $70 — your stake is now $700. But if bad news drops them to $30, you hold $300. Same shares, different story. The price is just what the crowd currently believes.

Diversification is the only free lunch in investing: spreading money across many assets means one failure can't sink you. Index funds do this automatically — one purchase buys tiny slices of hundreds of companies.

cards.q: What does owning a stock actually mean?
choices: You own a small slice of the company
cards.explain: Stock = equity = ownership. Lending the company money is a bond; working there is a job. Shareholders own a piece and share the profits (and losses).

flashcards.back: A small ownership slice of a company — a claim on a fraction of its profits.
Higher potential returns always come with higher risk. No exceptions.
Spreading money across many assets so one failure can't sink you.

flashcards.front: What does an index fund buy you?
flashcards.back: Tiny slices of hundreds of companies in one purchase — instant diversification.

questions.q: A company's profits double but its share price falls. Why might that happen?
questions.explain: Prices reflect expectations, not just results. Great news that falls short of great expectations still disappoints the crowd.

choices: A scam or a lie — risk and return always pair up
questions.explain: The risk-return tradeoff has no exceptions. High promised returns with 'no risk' is the oldest pitch in fraud.

questions.q: Why do index funds beat most professional stock-pickers over time?
choices: Tiny fees plus diversification across the whole market
questions.explain: Most active managers can't beat the market after fees. Index funds win by charging almost nothing and owning everything.

questions.q: What's the difference between a stock and a bond?
choices: Stock is ownership; a bond is a loan to the company
questions.explain: Buy a stock, you own a slice. Buy a bond, the company owes you money plus interest. Bonds are generally steadier — and capped.

questions.q: The market drops 20% in a month. The disciplined long-term move is:
choices: Stick to the plan — panic selling locks in losses
questions.explain: Market drops are the price of long-term returns. Selling in a panic turns a temporary dip into a permanent loss.
